title: Question 6: Right to Abortion Before Fetal Viability

context.text: Question 6 is Initiative Petition C-05-2023, a citizen-initiated amendment to Article 1 of the Nevada Constitution. Under Article 19, Section 2 of the Nevada Constitution, an initiative to amend the Constitution must be approved by voters at two successive general elections; this is the second vote, after November 2024, per the Legislative Counsel Bureau fiscal note.

Nevada Current reports voters approved Question 6 in 2024 with 64% support; News 3/News 4 reports abortion protections passed in 2024 by nearly 29 percentage points. It is one of two statewide questions on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot, the fewest since 2012 per News 3/News 4, and it keeps its 2024 number.
The Nevada Secretary of State's office released its official 2026 Ballot Question Guide on or about Sept. 29-30, 2026, per FOX5.

question.text: Should the Nevada Constitution be amended to create an individual's fundamental right to an abortion, without interference by state or local governments, whenever the abortion is performed by a qualified healthcare professional until fetal viability or when necessary to protect the health or life of the pregnant individual at any point during the pregnancy?

summary.text: Initiative Petition C-05-2023 would add a new section (Section 25 of Article 1, per the fiscal note) to the Nevada Constitution creating a right to abortion, performed by a qualified healthcare professional, from the start of pregnancy until fetal viability, or throughout pregnancy when needed to protect the life or health of the pregnant patient. State and local governments generally could not interfere with the right, except where a "compelling state interest" exists, which the explanation says occurs only if the government uses the least restrictive means to protect or improve the pregnant person's life or health in ways that follow clinical standards of practice. The digest describes existing law as legal abortion within 24 weeks of the start of pregnancy, with an exception after 24 weeks if a physician reasonably believes an abortion is necessary to preserve the pregnant person's life or health. Fiscal note (Legislative Counsel Bureau Fiscal Analysis Division, Aug. 1, 2024): the financial impact cannot be determined, because it is unknown which existing laws, if any, would not comply or how the Legislature would revise them. The committee argument in favor states that the measure has no fiscal or environmental impact; the committee argument against states that its cost cannot be determined.

measure.yesMeans: A "Yes" vote would create a new section of the Nevada Constitution to establish a person's constitutional right to abortion, so that a person can make decisions about matters relating to abortion and reproductive healthcare, without interference from state or local governments.
measure.noMeans: A "No" vote would keep the Nevada Constitution in its current form and would not impact the availability of abortion as a statutory right under Nevada law.

argumentsFor.text: Ballot Question Committee in favor (Lindsey Harmon, Chair; Denise Lopez; Bradley Schrager): "Decisions about abortion should be left to women and qualified healthcare professionals, who take a pledge to act in their patients' best interest."

Ballot Question Committee in favor (Lindsey Harmon, Chair; Denise Lopez; Bradley Schrager): "YES keeps families – not politicians – in charge of their own healthcare decisions, so that women can make these personal decisions in consultation with their doctors and those they love and trust."

argumentsAgainst.text: Ballot Question Committee opposed (Emily Mimnaugh, Chair; Jason Guinasso): "Question 6 has no bright-line rule saying when abortion is legal. Is it always legal at 4 months? 6 months? 9 months? Our current law is clear. Question 6 is not."
Ballot Question Committee opposed (Emily Mimnaugh, Chair; Jason Guinasso): "Vote NO to protect our current abortion law. Abortion is legal in Nevada."

researchNotes: Sources: nvsos.gov is behind bot protection (not bypassed); the official text was read instead from the Clark County Election Department's 'Ballot Questions, General Election November 3, 2026' PDF, which reproduces the question, Legislative Counsel explanation and digest, the Ballot Question Committee arguments and rebuttals, and the Fiscal Analysis Division fiscal note for both statewide questions. Note that the explanation/arguments/fiscal note in that 2026 county document are the 2024-era texts (fiscal notes dated July 29 and Aug. 1, 2024), since the same initiatives return unchanged for the second vote. Slate: the county document contains exactly two statewide questions (6 and 7); News 3/News 4 (July 2026) reports these are the only two statewide questions this year, with other petitions failing to qualify, and FOX5 (Sept. 30, 2026) reports the Secretary of State's official 2026 Ballot Question Guide covers these two. The nvsos.gov guide itself was not read. Arguments are excerpts of the official committee arguments (the pamphlet prints one argument for and one against, plus a rebuttal on each side), attributed to the committees as the document names them. Required vote: a majority of those voting at this second election.
